    RA("Research Agent"):::agent

    %% INNO System subgraph
    subgraph "INNO System"
        IC("INNO Core"):::innocore
        subgraph "Agents Module"
            IA("Agents (draft_agent,idea_agent,exp_analyser,judge_agent,ml_agent,plan_agent,prepare_agent,survey_agent)"):::agents

<explanation>
Below is a detailed explanation for drawing a system design diagram that highlights the workings of the INNO framework and the overall research agent. The focus is on decomposing the research automation pipeline—especially the INNO engine—and showing how the research agent uses it to drive scientific discovery. Here’s how to proceed:

1. Overall System Context:
   • Note that this project (“AI‑Researcher”) is a full research automation system with multiple modules. The diagram should reflect two high-level layers:
     – The Research Agent layer, which handles user queries (at Level 1 and Level 2), orchestrates research tasks, and commands paper writing.
     – The INNO engine, a module used by the research agent to execute the research workflow.
  
2. Main Components to Highlight:
   • Research Agent: This is the entry point for user inputs (detailed idea or references). Draw a box labelled “Research Agent” that includes command interfaces (e.g., run_infer_idea.py, run_infer_plan.py, and accompanying shell scripts). Indicate that it processes queries, selects the task level, and triggers the research workflow.
   • INNO Core: Represent the core orchestration engine (folder “research_agent/inno/”) as a central component. This core handles the logic for research task management.
   • INNO Agents: Cluster within the INNO system are a set of sub‐agents (such as draft_agent, idea_agent, exp_analyser, judge_agent, ml_agent, plan_agent, prepare_agent, survey_agent). Draw a sub-box or multiple adjacent boxes inside the “INNO” module labelled “Agents” with arrows mapping the responsibilities from “Idea Generation” → “Planning” → “Experimentation/Analysis” → “Drafting.”
   • Memory Modules: Include a box for “Memory” that covers components like code_memory, code_tree_memory, paper_memory, rag_memory, and tool_memory (from research_agent/inno/memory). This shows how previous research artifacts and context are stored and re‐used.
   • Environment Interfaces: Represent the “Environment” submodule (research_agent/inno/environment) that includes browser environment, docker container interfaces, TCP server, cookies handling, and markdown browser. Use arrows to indicate that these components interface with external systems.
   • Tools: Create another box for “Tools” (research_agent/inno/tools, including specialized ones such as arxiv_source, Github operations, file surfing, etc.). These tools act to connect to external research databases and code repositories.
   • Workflow: Optionally, include a “Workflow” component (research_agent/inno/workflow) that shows the dynamic flow—like flowgraph and flowcache—used to schedule and propagate research tasks.
  
3. Data Flow and Interactions:
   • Draw directional arrows from “Research Agent” to the “INNO Core” indicating that upon receiving a query, the research agent passes the input to INNO.
   • Within the INNO block, show arrows from the core to the Agents. You can annotate these arrows with tasks such as “Generate ideas,” “Plan experiments,” “Prepare proposals” (which are handled by idea_agent, plan_agent, etc.).
   • Connect the Agents block to the Memory module, demonstrating that agents refer to stored code trees, previous paper drafts, and other past work.
   • Illustrate connections from the Agents to the Environment box. This shows that during its operations, agents need to connect with external environments (e.g., to retrieve papers, use docker containers for execution, or fetch browser data).
   • Connect Tools to both INNO and Environment—since tools serve as the bridge to external APIs (e.g., GitHub, arXiv, and other research databases). 
   • Include feedback loops: For example, upon experiment validation, results are stored back into the Memory module and then influence subsequent iterations.
  
4. Architectural Style & Diagram Components:
   • Use clearly labelled boxes for each component (Research Agent, INNO Core, Agents, Memory, Environment, Tools, Workflow).
   • Use directional arrows to indicate data flow:
     – From user input → Research Agent → INNO.
     – Within INNO, arrows showing task delegation to different Agents.
     – From Agents to Environment and Tools for accessing external data.
     – Feedback arrows from Memory to INNO Core for iterative refinements.
   • Optionally apply color coding or distinct shapes:
     – For instance, use rounded rectangles for agents, cylinders for memory (representing storage), and parallelograms for environment interfaces.
  
5. Tailoring to the Specific Project:
   • Emphasize that the “INNO” module is at the heart of the research automation process. It structures the pipeline that the research agent triggers.
   • Map out the workflow: the research agent receives a query (differentiating between a detailed idea description versus reference-based ideation) and then selects an appropriate execution mode (as indicated in the shell scripts shown in the README). Then it calls the INNO Core, which in turn activates various agents that (a) generate ideas, (b) analyze experiments, (c) plan research steps, and (d) draft results.
   • Underline that the diagram should capture the abstraction levels (user input → orchestration → execution using external tools/environments) with iterative loops.
  
6. Final Instructions:
   • The diagram should be detailed—include a minimum of seven distinct components (Research Agent, INNO Core, Agents, Memory, Environment, Tools, Workflow).
   • Use directional arrows and label them with notes such as “query processing,” “task delegation,” “data retrieval,” “feedback loop,” etc.
   • Use clear labels and possibly color-code each component type so that one can immediately distinguish processing logic (agents/core), storage (memory), external interactions (environment/tools), and orchestration (research agent and workflow).
   • Keep the focus on how the research agent utilizes the INNO subsystem: show the aggregation of various INNO agents that perform specialized sub-tasks, how they share memory, and how they interface with external systems via designated environment adapters and tool modules.
  
This breakdown gives you all the essential elements to build an architecture diagram that communicates both the modular design and the dynamic interplay between the research agent and the INNO system. This detailed diagram will be invaluable for understanding the automated research discovery process implemented by AI‑Researcher.
</explanation>
